y-m-59-13.title: If the log value is larger, is the argument larger too?
y-m-59-13.topic: Logarithmic inequalities and the range of the base
y-m-59-13.goal: Confirm with cases that comparing the size of logarithms depends on the range of the base, state the condition under which the claim 'if the log value is larger, x is larger too' holds, and build examples for the two cases yourself.
y-m-59-13.material:
Jaehee said, "If log_a x > log_a 3, then x > 3." (Reading: if log base a of x is greater than log base a of 3.) The base a is a > 0, a ≠ 1, and the argument x is x > 0.

The table has a few values.
Base 2: log_2 1 = 0, log_2 2 = 1, log_2 4 = 2, log_2 3 ≈ 1.58
Base 1/2: log_(1/2) 1 = 0, log_(1/2) 2 = −1, log_(1/2) 4 = −2, log_(1/2) 3 ≈ −1.58
y-m-59-13.thinking.0: Examine the conditions under which a generalized claim holds
y-m-59-13.thinking.1: Split into cases by the range of the base
y-m-59-13.prereq.0: The 'H2' of this task is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Assumption: it is solved by a student who has already learned the content below.
y-m-59-13.prereq.1: The meaning of logarithm (log_a x is the power to which you raise a to get x) and the domain (a > 0, a ≠ 1, x > 0)
y-m-59-13.prereq.2: The graph shapes (increasing, decreasing) of logarithmic functions with a base greater than 1 and with a base less than 1
y-m-59-13.prereq.3: Finding values like log_2 4 = 2 and log_(1/2) 4 = −2
y-m-59-13.s.s1.prompt: Judge Jaehee's claim by looking at the values in the table.
y-m-59-13.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the log values of the same two arguments (for example 2 and 3) when the base is 2 and when it is 1/2.
y-m-59-13.s.s1.hint.1: In each of the two columns of the table, check whether the value gets larger or smaller as the argument gets larger.
y-m-59-13.s.s1.o.a: It depends on the base. There are cases where it is true and cases where it is false
y-m-59-13.s.s1.r.a: You compared two cases with different bases and judged that a condition is needed. The next job is to sort out which conclusion comes out for which base.
y-m-59-13.s.s1.o.b: It is true. For a logarithm, the larger the argument, the larger the value always
y-m-59-13.s.s1.r.b: You generalized only the case where the base is 2. Check how the value changes as the argument gets larger in the base 1/2 column of the table.
y-m-59-13.s.s1.o.c: It is false. With this inequality, x is always less than 3
y-m-59-13.s.s1.r.c: You missed the table value in the base 2 case (log_2 4 > log_2 3). Check the case in base 2 where x is greater than 3.
y-m-59-13.s.s1.o.d: Knowing the value of x is enough and the base has nothing to do with the judgment
y-m-59-13.s.s1.r.d: Check the case where, even if x is the same, a different base changes the direction of the inequality sign.
y-m-59-13.s.s1.explain: In base 2, log_2 4 > log_2 3 and 4 > 3, which matches the claim. In base 1/2, log_(1/2) 2 = −1 > log_(1/2) 3 ≈ −1.58 but 2 < 3, so the claim breaks. So it depends on the base.
y-m-59-13.s.s2.prompt: Make two different (a, x) that satisfy the inequality log_a x > log_a 3, so that one example uses an x greater than 3 and the other uses an x less than 3. (a > 0, a ≠ 1, x > 0)
y-m-59-13.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a base, find the two log values, and check which is larger.
y-m-59-13.s.s2.hint.1: Test in what range you should choose the base to make x less than 3.
y-m-59-13.s.s2.ok.c1: The base and the argument are within the domain.
y-m-59-13.s.s2.fail.c1: The base must be a > 0, a ≠ 1, and the argument must be x > 0.
y-m-59-13.s.s2.fail.c2: The direction of the inequality sign depends on whether the base is greater than or less than 1. Find the two log values yourself and compare.
y-m-59-13.s.s2.explain: If the base is greater than 1, the larger the argument, the larger the log value, so x > 3 is needed, and if the base is between 0 and 1, the larger the argument, the smaller the log value, so 0 < x < 3 is needed. Example: (2, 4) gives 2 > 1.58, and (0.5, 2) gives −1 > −1.58.
y-m-59-13.s.s3.prompt: Fix Jaehee's claim. Write one sentence each for the solution of the inequality log_a x > log_a 3 according to the range of the base a.
y-m-59-13.s.s3.hint.0: First write the solutions separately for when the base is 2 and when it is 1/2.
y-m-59-13.s.s3.hint.1: Rewrite the two cases in general words (base greater than 1 / base less than 1).
y-m-59-13.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When the base is greater than 1, ..., and when the base is between 0 and 1, ...
y-m-59-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write it without leaving out the argument condition x > 0?
y-m-59-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the reason 'when the base is less than 1, the direction of the inequality sign flips' to the log values increasing or decreasing?
y-m-59-13.s.s3.model.0: If a > 1, the logarithm increases, so x > 3, and if 0 < a < 1, the logarithm decreases, so the direction of the inequality sign flips and 0 < x < 3. The argument must be positive, so we must also keep x > 0.
y-m-59-13.s.s3.model.1: If the base is greater than 1, it holds when x is greater than 3. If the base is greater than 0 and less than 1, it holds when x is less than 3, but x must be greater than 0.

y-m-59-14.title: Do 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … stay below 1?
y-m-59-14.topic: Limits of sequences and infinite decimals
y-m-59-14.goal: Find the error of concluding that a limit is also less than a number just because every term is less than that number, and explain the limit as the difference getting endlessly close to 0.
y-m-59-14.material: Consider the sequence S₁ = 0.9, S₂ = 0.99, S₃ = 0.999, …. Sₙ is the number with n nines after the decimal point. The value this sequence gets endlessly close to is written 0.999…. Jiho claimed "0.999… is less than 1" and argued as below.
y-m-59-14.thinking.0: Check the logic of an intuitive claim
y-m-59-14.thinking.1: Find the line with the error
y-m-59-14.thinking.2: Explain a limit through the change in the difference
y-m-59-14.prereq.0: The 'H2' of this task is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the course to a particular grade. Assumption: it is solved by a student who has already learned the content below.
y-m-59-14.prereq.1: The meaning of the limit of a sequence: the terms get endlessly close to a number
y-m-59-14.prereq.2: The geometric sequence (1/10)^n getting close to 0
y-m-59-14.prereq.3: The agreement that the infinite decimal 0.999… is the value that 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … head toward
y-m-59-14.s.s1.prompt: First judge Jiho's claim '0.999… is less than 1'.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.hint.0: Find the difference between 1 and each of S₁, S₂, S₃.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.hint.1: Observe what happens to that difference as n gets larger.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.o.a: It is right. No term becomes 1, so the limit is also less than 1
y-m-59-14.s.s1.r.a: You carried a property of the terms over to a property of the limit as it is. Examine whether the limit must have the same property as the terms.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.o.b: I can't judge. 0.999… is not a number but a process that keeps changing
y-m-59-14.s.s1.r.b: You saw an infinite decimal only as a 'changing process'. This task agreed that 0.999… is the value the sequence gets endlessly close to.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.o.c: It is wrong. The limit is 1, so 0.999… and 1 are the same number
y-m-59-14.s.s1.r.c: You told apart the terms and the limit. The evidence for whether this judgment is right (the change in the difference) is checked in the following steps.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.o.d: 0.999… is a separate number that is neither less than nor greater than 1
y-m-59-14.s.s1.r.d: You did not settle the size relationship between 1 and 0.999…. Think about whether another number could fit between the two numbers.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.explain: This judgment is still a guess. Let's check what the fact 'every term is less than 1' says about the limit by checking the argument below line by line.
y-m-59-14.s.s1.acc.0: At first, it is natural to think this way by intuition. Let's check whether this judgment is right by checking the argument below line by line.
y-m-59-14.s.s2.prompt: Choose one unjustified line in Jiho's argument that jumps to the conclusion.
y-m-59-14.s.s2.hint.0: Check how each line follows from the line before it.
y-m-59-14.s.s2.hint.1: Test with another sequence (for example 1 − 1/n) whether 'every term is less than 1' and 'the limit is less than 1' mean the same thing.
y-m-59-14.s.s2.line.1: (1/10)^n is always greater than 0, so Sₙ < 1 for every n.
y-m-59-14.s.s2.line.2: Every term is less than 1, so the value 0.999… that these terms get endlessly close to must also be less than 1.
y-m-59-14.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is unjustified. Even if every term is less than 1, its limit can be 1. For example, every term of 1 − 1/n is less than 1, but the limit is 1. Lines 1 and 2 are right, and line 4 just carries over the conclusion of line 3.
y-m-59-14.s.s3.prompt: Using what happens to 1 − Sₙ = (1/10)^n as n gets larger, explain the relationship between 0.999… and 1 in one or two sentences.
y-m-59-14.s.s3.hint.0: Write the values of 1 − Sₙ for n = 1, 2, 3.
y-m-59-14.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence what happens to those values as n gets larger.
y-m-59-14.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The difference between 1 and Sₙ is ...
y-m-59-14.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write why the difference getting close to 0 leads to the conclusion that it equals 1?
y-m-59-14.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart why the fact 'every term is less than 1' does not contradict the conclusion (the limit is not a term)?
y-m-59-14.s.s3.model.0: The difference between 1 and Sₙ is (1/10)^n, and the larger n gets, the closer it gets to 0 endlessly. So the value Sₙ gets endlessly close to is 1, and 0.999… equals 1. Each term is less than 1, but the limit can be different from the terms.
y-m-59-14.s.s3.model.1: There is no number that can fit between 1 and 0.999…, and the difference gets endlessly small like (1/10)^n, so the two are the same number. Each term not being 1 and the limit being 1 do not contradict each other.
